HarnessTTT: Learn to Optimize Harness at Test-Time for Scientific Discovery

Yingzi Ma Affiliation: University of Wisconsin-Madison    Yulong Cao Affiliation: NVIDIA    Nanxi Li Affiliation: Johns Hopkins University    Fang Wu Affiliation: Stanford University    Yizhe Zhang Affiliation: Meta    James Zou Affiliation: Stanford University    Yejin Choi Affiliation: Stanford University    Chaowei Xiao Affiliation: Johns Hopkins University
Abstract

Scientific discovery with language models requires finding the best valid solution within a finite computational budget. We study how feedback from this search can improve the procedure used to conduct it. We introduce HarnessTTT, a test-time learning framework that trains a harness proposer while keeping the executor frozen. The proposer generates executable harnesses comprising system prompts, reusable skills, tools, middleware, and execution controls. Each harness guides a budgeted discovery rollout, whose outcome provides feedback for updating the proposer. A discovery-oriented policy-gradient objective combines gap-normalized rewards, leave-one-out advantages (RLOO), and max-sharpening to favor high-performing proposals. Generated components are validated before execution, and the search retains the best valid solution and selected harnesses across rounds. Across fourteen discovery tasks in mathematics, systems, GPU kernels, heuristic programming, astrodynamics, and biology, HarnessTTT with a frozen 9B executor improves on OpenEvolve with the same executor on all eleven benchmark tasks (e.g., from 1.17 to 2.64 on circle packing), improves on the discovery-fine-tuned Finch-9B by up to 92%92\%, holds the best open-weight sub-10B result on nine, and reaches 0.3809190.380919 on Erdős minimum overlap, better than the best human reference of 0.3809270.380927. Scaling the proposer and frozen executor to 27B improves on eleven of fourteen tasks, and transferring the learned harnesses to GPT-5.5 matches or exceeds the strongest reported system of any backbone on nine of fourteen tasks. Together, these results show that harness search can itself be learned at test time: a trained proposer lets a small frozen executor search effectively, and the harnesses it finds carry over to stronger executors.

1 Introduction

Scientific discovery advances knowledge and technology by finding solutions beyond what established methods can achieve [52, 42]. Recent work [77, 72, 65] on AI for scientific discovery formulates each task as an exploration for the best valid solution to a single challenging scientific problem within a finite computational budget, with the hope of surpassing the best-known results from the best human expert [14]. Success is therefore measured by the best solution found during the exploration, rather than the average quality of all attempts.

Large language models have tackled these tasks through two representative routes as shown in Figure 3. TTT-Discover [77] performs reinforcement learning at test time [3, 87], directly updating the executor—the model that solves the task—from its search outcomes guided by the reward. This adapts the model to solve the problem directly, but requires repeated sampling and training, with 25,600 rollouts per problem in its reported configuration (50 rounds ×\times 512 rollouts). Moreover, the learned behavioral adaptation remains encoded in the executor’s parameters, making individual changes difficult to isolate and limiting their direct transfer to a different or stronger executor. Artifact evolution methods [52, 42, 58, 28, 72] instead keep the executor and harness fixed—adaptation occurs through the feedback artifacts supplied in context. Artifacts are inspectable and reusable, allowing subsequent attempts to build on previous discoveries. However, adaptation within the search occurs through the artifacts supplied in context: the model must infer useful revisions based on its in-context capabilities [59, 38], without parameter updates from these outcomes. In long-horizon discovery, successive rounds produce increasingly extensive histories. When more of this history is incorporated into the input, accumulating more experience does not reliably translate into more effective exploration [32, 18].

To address the above limitations, we introduce HarnessTTT, which updates the proposer’s parameters to generate and refine task-specific harnesses while keeping the executor frozen (as shown in Figure 2). Our approach takes inspiration from human researchers, who improve not only the solutions they explore, but also the harness through which they explore them. During the exploration, humans may develop reusable problem-solving skills, revise construction methods, build specialized tools, or reorganize the experimental workflow to improve exploration efficiency. On a circle-packing problem, for example, a researcher might adopt a boundary-first construction strategy, write tools that check pairwise overlaps and boundary violations or compute the largest radii a fixed set of centers admits, and organize geometric diagnostics to guide subsequent refinements. In an agentic system, these changes correspond to adapting the complete harness that governs the executor’s behavior [71, 67, 29]. These harness-level adaptations shape an entire subsequent sequence of attempts, rather than only the next candidate solution.

HarnessTTT makes such harness adaptation a learned process as shown in Figure 4. At each round, unlike existing methods that adapt only part of the harness—a prompt or context playbook [70, 24, 1, 83], a code patch installed at predefined lifecycle hooks of a fixed runtime [56], or a fixed four-module protocol (memory, planning, action, and tool/skill orchestration) that draws on a given tool and skill registry [79]—our proposer model generates complete harnesses comprising system prompts, skills, tools, middleware, and execution-control parameters. Each generated harness guides the frozen executor through a budgeted discovery rollout from a shared incumbent solution. Improvements in the best valid solution provide rewards, which update the proposer’s parameters via our carefully designed reinforcement learning methods, while only the selected best solution, the incumbent harness, and a compact experience digest are retained for the next round. Across rounds, discovery experience changes the proposer’s policy itself, enabling reliable improvement via learning. Meanwhile, the resulting harness remains explicit and separate from the executor’s weights: it can be inspected, revised, and deployed with a stronger executor, providing a mechanism for weak-to-strong transfer [7].

Implementing HarnessTTT presents two challenges. First, harness-level credit assignment is indirect and noisy. The proposer generates a harness rather than a final solution, so its reward is observed only through a separate, stochastic executor rollout. Even when a fixed solution has a deterministic score, the same harness can produce different trajectories and yield different best solutions. The observed reward therefore reflects both harness quality and executor sampling variability. We develop a discovery-oriented RLOO-based update [25, 2] with gap-normalized rewards, leave-one-out advantages without variance normalization [34], max-sharpening [54, 6], and filtering of uninformative groups [74], designed to limit noise amplification while accommodating heterogeneous reward scales and best-of-group selection. Second, harness optimization must guard against reward hacking and information leakage. Higher evaluator scores do not necessarily reflect better solutions: an agent may exploit flaws in the evaluation process [26, 39] or use information unavailable under the intended task protocol [23]. We therefore design a new critic component to address this challenge.

We evaluate HarnessTTT on fourteen discovery problems spanning mathematical constructions [42, 14], systems benchmarks [9], GPU kernels [77], heuristic programming contests [4, 22], astrodynamics, and biology. With a frozen Qwen3.5-9B executor [49], HarnessTTT improves on OpenEvolve with the same executor on all eleven benchmark tasks and holds the best open-weight sub-10B result on nine, ahead of the discovery-fine-tuned Finch-9B [30] on every task by up to 91.7%91.7\%. Scaling the proposer and the frozen executor to Qwen3.8-27B [50] improves on eleven of fourteen tasks, and transferring the learned harnesses to GPT-5.5 matches or exceeds the strongest reported system of any backbone on nine of fourteen tasks and comes within 1%1\% on four more. Our ablations show where the gains come from: at matched rollouts, routing reward into the proposer’s weights reaches better results earlier than updating the executor or the proposer’s context; wider search per round yields late breakthroughs; and our RLOO objective with max-sharpening outperforms standard GRPO and a frozen proposer. Together, these results show that the search procedure itself can be learned at test time with a small frozen model and carried over to stronger executors.

2 Related Work

\para

Self-evolution by adapting the model. One family improves an agent by changing model weights. Test-time training and test-time RL adapt weights per instance or per problem [3, 87], while test-time scaling spends more inference compute [40]; for discovery, TTT-Discover [77] and ThetaEvolve [65] fine-tune the executor on its own search rollouts and hold strong published ≤\leq10B records, while discovery fine-tuning amortizes the skill across tasks by training on evolution-trajectory corpora, as in the Finch models we use as a parameter-matched comparator [30]. Closest to us, HASE [36] and SIA [17] co-evolve weights and harness, which couples the improver to the improved and requires update access to the executor; HarnessTTT freezes the executor and trains a separate proposer policy.

\para

Self-evolution by editing the harness. A second family keeps the model frozen and revises an external artifact. Evolutionary program search around frozen LLMs produces state-of-the-art discovery programs: FunSearch [52], AlphaEvolve [42, 14], open reimplementations and successors [58, 28], heuristic evolution [31], equation discovery [60], reward design [37], and multi-agent and meta-evolution systems [48, 33], evaluated on algorithm-engineering suites [22] and the systems problems of Cheng et al. [9]; research agents automate the surrounding pipeline [35]. A parallel line lets a frozen model rewrite its own code or scaffold: STOP [78], the Darwin Gödel Machine [81], self-improving coding agents [51, 73], capability-synthesizing generalists [47], and a survey of the space [13]. A third optimizes the text or structure around the model: prompt search [86, 70, 12, 16, 62], prompt compilation [24, 45], textual gradients [76, 10], reflective evolution [1], automated agent and workflow design [20, 82, 55, 85], whole-harness editing [29, 80], and in-context self-correction [64, 59, 38]. Across this family the proposer’s weights are fixed, so design knowledge is re-derived per task rather than accumulated. We train the proposer across rounds, and its action space includes executable tool code: unlike tool creation that abstracts functions from solution traces [8, 46, 75, 66], the tools here are emitted by a learned policy and admitted through a leak-limiting review chain (§3.2).

3 HarnessTTT

HarnessTTT learns the discovery procedure by training a harness proposer while keeping the executor frozen. The proposer specifies how the executor searches through proposed harnesses; the executor conducts budgeted rollouts to generate candidate solutions and interacts with evaluators to obtain scores for them. Feedback from these evaluators updates the proposer and the search state retained between rounds. We first formulate the discovery objective, then describe the harness representation, proposer update, iterative search, and validation protocol.

\para

Problem formulation and framework overview. A task τ\tau provides a description dτd_{\tau}, a seed program x0x_{0} with a marked editable region, and a black-box evaluator mτm_{\tau}; the seed program and evaluator are taken from Lee et al. [30]. Each rollout may call the evaluator at most BB times. An agent pairs a frozen language-model executor M0M_{0} with an executable harness HH that governs how M0M_{0} interacts with the task. Each outer round starts from a search state: the incumbent program x⋆x^{\star} (the best found so far, initially x0x_{0}) with score bτ=mτ​(x⋆)b_{\tau}=m_{\tau}(x^{\star}), the incumbent harness H⋆H^{\star}, and an experience digest DD.

Given this context, the proposer πϕ\pi_{\phi} samples KK harness specifications. Each round keeps a single incumbent harness H⋆H^{\star}, but proposals are dealt round-robin between H⋆H^{\star} and one diversity-preserving runner-up parent: the best candidate within 2% of the top score that adds a new component, or else the second-highest scorer. This keeps components from non-winning candidates alive for another round [1, 81]. In the first round all KK proposals share the initial harness. Each specification is merged into its parent, validated, and compiled into a candidate harness HkH_{k}; all candidates start from the same program x⋆x^{\star}. Only the proposer’s LoRA adapter ϕ\phi is trained [19]; M0M_{0} is never updated. A rollout of M0M_{0} under HkH_{k} edits the program and calls the evaluator on programs xk,1,…,xk,Tx_{k,1},\dots,x_{k,T} (T≤BT\leq B); its score is the best valid score it finds, sk=maxt≤T⁡mτ​(xk,t)s_{k}=\max_{t\leq T}m_{\tau}(x_{k,t}), where invalid programs are skipped and a rollout without any valid program counts as failed. The round keeps the best solution found, so the proposer’s objective is the best score in the group, never below the incumbent’s: JK​(ϕ)=𝔼πϕ​[max⁡(bτ,s1,…,sK)]J_{K}(\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\phi}}[\max(b_{\tau},s_{1},\dots,s_{K})]. The update in §3.1 is a group-relative surrogate that favors high-scoring proposals, not an unbiased gradient of JKJ_{K}.

\para

Executable harness representation. What the proposer can learn is bounded by what a harness can express. Existing systems represent it narrowly: prompt optimizers rewrite instructions [12, 24, 1], reflective agents append notes to the context [59, 83], and Harness-R1 patches a fixed runtime without adding executable tools [56]. These change what the executor is told but not what it can do, such as adding an analysis tool or restarting a stalled search. We instead represent the harness as an executable program built on NexAU [41] with five editable components (Figure 8; Appendix C): a system prompt for strategy and workflow, skills for reusable procedures, tools including proposer-written Python functions, middleware hooks that run between executor steps (e.g., budget reminders, restarts after stalls), and control parameters for sampling and iteration limits. The proposer edits a private copy of H⋆H^{\star} and cannot touch the task program, evaluator, executor weights, or shared runtime; unchanged fields are inherited, so a partial specification still yields a complete harness. Each episode ends with validate_harness, which checks schemas, mounts, and generated code (§3.2), and submit_harness; accepted specifications are compiled and hashed to remove duplicates within the group. The result is a standalone artifact that can be inspected or run with another frozen executor (§4.5).

3.1 Learning the harness proposer

A harness is judged only through executor rollouts. Even with a deterministic evaluator, the same harness can lead a stochastic executor to different solutions. An observed score therefore mixes the quality of a proposed procedure with downstream sampling variability. Our RLOO-based update [2, 25] must assign credit under this indirect feedback while accounting for shrinking absolute gains and an objective that retains the best discovery rather than the average attempt.

\para

Reward. As search approaches a strong reference, meaningful improvements can become small in absolute units. With an unnormalized leave-one-out advantage, these smaller score differences carry less policy-gradient weight even when they close the same fraction of the remaining gap. A valid candidate is rewarded by how much its rollout score sks_{k} improves on the incumbent score bτb_{\tau}, relative to the remaining gap to a published reference score uτu_{\tau} (listed in the appendix), or to |bτ||b_{\tau}| once the incumbent has reached it:

gk=sk−bτZτ,Zτ={uτ−bτ,bτ<uτ−ϵ,|bτ|+ϵ,otherwise.g_{k}=\frac{s_{k}-b_{\tau}}{Z_{\tau}},\qquad Z_{\tau}=\begin{cases}u_{\tau}-b_{\tau},&b_{\tau}<u_{\tau}-\epsilon,\\ |b_{\tau}|+\epsilon,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (1)

A small remaining gap can make a large gain produce an extreme normalized reward. We smoothly cap positive credit below the reference, while retaining graded penalties for rollouts that underperform the incumbent:

rk={3​tanh⁡(gk/3),bτ<uτ−ϵ,gk>0,max⁡{−1,gk},bτ<uτ−ϵ,gk≤0,clip⁡(gk,−1,5),otherwise,r_{k}=\begin{cases}3\tanh(g_{k}/3),&b_{\tau}<u_{\tau}-\epsilon,\ g_{k}>0,\\ \max\{-1,\,g_{k}\},&b_{\tau}<u_{\tau}-\epsilon,\ g_{k}\leq 0,\\ \operatorname{clip}(g_{k},-1,5),&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} (2)

with ϵ=10−9\epsilon=10^{-9}. Below the reference, gains are smoothly capped, losses are linear and floored at −1-1, and matching the incumbent earns zero; invalid, failed, or repaired candidates receive −1-1. The reference uτu_{\tau} is used only for the reward and is never shown to the executor or written into a harness.

Proposals inherit different harness parents, so a cross-parent comparison could reward an inherited advantage rather than the proposed revision. We compute advantages within groups 𝒢\mathcal{G} sharing a parent and prompt: one group of size Kg=KK_{g}=K in the first round, then two groups of size Kg=K/2K_{g}=K/2. Within each group, valid rewards spanning less than δ=10−3\delta=10^{-3} are replaced by their mean to avoid crediting near-tied outcomes. Denoting the resulting rewards by r~k\widetilde{r}_{k}, we compute the leave-one-out advantage AkLOO=r~k−1Kg−1​∑j∈𝒢∖{k}r~j.A_{k}^{\mathrm{LOO}}=\widetilde{r}_{k}-\frac{1}{K_{g}-1}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{G}\setminus\{k\}}\widetilde{r}_{j}. We omit division by the group’s reward standard deviation, which can turn small, potentially noisy differences into order-one advantages [34, 57]. The RLOO term thus retains the task-relative magnitude established by gap normalization. All-valid tied groups are excluded from training [74]; groups receiving identical status penalties are assigned zero advantages and skipped before computing a valid-reward range or temperature. Mixed groups preserve the contrast between tied valid rewards and status penalties. To additionally favor the strongest outcomes retained by the discovery objective, we augment RLOO with a centered softmax sharpening term [54, 6]:

Ak=(1−α)​AkLOO+α⁡[softmax⁡(𝐫~𝒢/T𝒢)k−1Kg],T𝒢=max⁡{Δ𝒢/4,ϵ},A_{k}=(1-\alpha)A_{k}^{\mathrm{LOO}}+\alpha\left[\operatorname{softmax}(\widetilde{\mathbf{r}}_{\mathcal{G}}/T_{\mathcal{G}})_{k}-\frac{1}{K_{g}}\right],\quad T_{\mathcal{G}}=\max\{\Delta_{\mathcal{G}}/4,\epsilon\}, (3)

where α=0.3\alpha=0.3, 𝐫~𝒢\widetilde{\mathbf{r}}_{\mathcal{G}} contains the group’s processed rewards, and Δ𝒢\Delta_{\mathcal{G}} is its valid-reward range. The two terms serve complementary purposes: RLOO preserves the magnitude of relative progress, while range-scaled sharpening emphasizes within-group ranking without reducing feedback to a hard winner label. Near-tie processing suppresses differences below the threshold, but does not distinguish genuine gains from executor noise. The combined advantage is a discovery-oriented heuristic and, like standard GRPO [57], not an unbiased gradient estimator.

\para

Proposer update. The executor generates the solutions, but the proposer generates the action being optimized. We therefore apply AkA_{k} only to the proposer-generated tokens in episode kk, masking tool observations and all executor tokens. With ρk,t​(ϕ)\rho_{k,t}(\phi) the ratio of current to sampling-policy token probabilities and 𝒯k\mathcal{T}_{k} the retained token set, we minimize the clipped surrogate [53] with a KL penalty toward the frozen base proposer πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}:

ℒ(ϕ)=−1N∑k∑t∈𝒯kmin(ρk,tAk,clip(ρk,t,1−ϵc,1+ϵc)Ak)+βℒKL,\mathcal{L}(\phi)=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{k}}\min\!\big(\rho_{k,t}A_{k},\ \operatorname{clip}(\rho_{k,t},1-\epsilon_{c},1+\epsilon_{c})A_{k}\big)+\beta\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}}, (4)

where N=∑k|𝒯k|N=\sum_{k}|\mathcal{T}_{k}|, ϵc\epsilon_{c} is the framework default, and ℒKL\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}} is the low-variance estimator πref/πϕ−log⁡(πref/πϕ)−1\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}/\pi_{\phi}-\log(\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}/\pi_{\phi})-1 with β=0.1\beta=0.1. Clipping and the KL anchor constrain the change made from a small batch of indirect feedback. Zero-advantage episodes are omitted; if no training tokens remain, the optimizer step is skipped without interrupting state retention. The persistent rank-64 LoRA adapter is trained for three epochs per round with learning rate 10−510^{-5} and batch size 8. Episodes are truncated to 18k tokens while preserving the final submission. The updated adapter then proposes the next round’s harnesses, closing the learning loop without changing M0M_{0}.

3.2 Experience retention and harness validation

\para

Incumbent and bounded context. At the end of each round, the best valid program in the group and its harness become the new incumbent if they strictly improve on its score (Figure 4; Appendix E), and the next round starts from them rather than from the seed. Solution quality therefore accumulates, and rewards measure progress beyond the current starting point. Under a fixed evaluator the incumbent score never decreases, but this follows from retention and does not by itself show that the proposer improved. Unlike reflective methods [59, 1], we do not feed the proposer the history of earlier candidates. Such a history grows every round, raises cost, and buries informative outcomes in a long context that models use poorly [32]. Feedback that drifts across rounds would also make within-group reward differences reflect context rather than proposer quality. The proposer instead reads a fixed-size experience digest, rebuilt each round: the incumbent harness and program (truncated), the seed and current best scores, and a stall flag. Experience across rounds is thus carried by the digest and the proposer’s weights. Proposals from the same parent share this digest and differ only in sampling seed.

\para

Harness validation. Evaluator scores cannot tell real improvements from exploits of the evaluation interface [61, 26, 11, 5, 84], so every generated tool is validated before rollouts. The critic in Figure 4 is this validation pipeline, not a learned value function. Tools access the task only through a restricted interface that withholds the evaluator implementation, ground truth, and network access, and they must pass static checks and a sandboxed self-test. A failing tool gets at most two repair attempts, screened for evaluator or target-score content, and is dropped if it still fails. These controls describe the evaluated protocol, not an independently verified guarantee.

4 Experiments

4.1 Evaluation Design

\para

Task suites. The parameter-matched comparison with open-weight systems (Table 1) uses the eleven tasks for which Finch-9B reports results [30]: five mathematical construction tasks (Erdős, AC1, AC2, CP26, Hadamard) [42, 14, 58]; two heuristic-contest programming tasks (AHC039, AHC058) scored under the official AtCoder 150-case protocol [4, 22]; and four systems algorithm design tasks (EPLB, PRISM, LLM-SQL, Txn) from the ADRS suite [9]. The ablation (Table 2) adds one astrodynamics task (V2) and one biological denoising task (scRNA) [72, 77], for thirteen tasks. The comparison with all prior methods (Table 3) further includes TriMul, the GPU MODE outgoing Triangle Multiplicative Update kernel benchmark, scored by geometric-mean latency across seven fixed input shapes on an NVIDIA H100 (lower is better) [77, 72], for fourteen tasks. TriMul (H100), V2 and scRNA have no external comparator under the open-model scale rule, and LLM-SQL and Txn are shown for disclosure and reported with caveats.

\para

Evaluation protocol. Following the default setting of Finch [30], every task provides a description, a seed program with a delimited editable region, a black-box evaluator, and a hard per-rollout evaluator-call budget. Tables report native metrics and mark their optimization direction. The configured executor interface exposes neither evaluator code nor ground truth (§3.2).

\para

Implementation and reporting unit. The principal executor is frozen Qwen3.5-9B [49] served with vLLM [27]; the scale comparison uses frozen Qwen3.8-27B [50]. The standard configuration runs 20 outer rounds and samples K=32K{=}32 (Qwen3.5-9B) or K=8K{=}8 (Qwen3.8-27B) harnesses per round; for each harness, the executor runs a single solution trajectory and may call the evaluator at most B=20B{=}20 (Qwen3.5-9B) or B=5B{=}5 (Qwen3.8-27B) times within it; the proposer is a persistent LoRA adapter [19] trained with our proposed advantage (Eq. 3) for three epochs per round at batch size 8 under a KL anchor. Tables report the selected valid outcome of each single search campaign, not an across-campaign mean; reruns of a selected program characterize execution noise only.

4.2 Results

\para

Open-weight ≤\leq10B regime. Table 1 compares HarnessTTT-9B with every open-weight system of at most 10B parameters that reports these tasks. With the same frozen Qwen3.5-9B executor, HarnessTTT-9B improves on OpenEvolve on all eleven tasks, e.g., from 1.173 to 2.636 on CP26 and from 134.5 to 713.6 on AHC058. It also improves on the discovery-fine-tuned Finch-9B on all eleven, by up to 91.7% on Hadamard and 36.2% on CP26. It holds the best ≤\leq10B value on nine tasks, including Hadamard, where its 0.921 is 60% above the next best (0.576, ThetaEvolve), and a tie at 2.635983 on CP26 with the three executor-updating systems. It trails on two: AC2, where those three systems reach 0.946–0.947 versus 0.934, and Txn, where Finch-4B reaches 4,762 versus 4,255. OpenEvolve with proprietary executors (Claude Opus 4.6, Gemini 3 Pro, GPT-5; Table 1) reports results on six of these tasks. HarnessTTT-9B matches or exceeds the best of them on five, and falls behind only on Txn. This suggests that a learned harness can close much of the gap between a small open-weight executor and far larger proprietary ones, without updating the executor. On AC2, the reported scores of ThetaEvolve and TTT-Discover are higher than HarnessTTT-9B. However, we find that this comparison is confounded by the initial program: on AC2, both methods start from a hand-designed program that scores far above ours, whereas on the other tasks the initial programs also differ but their initial scores are close to ours. Since the initial program’s score strongly affects subsequent evolution, we further discuss the effect of initial-program differences on discovery in §4.4.

\para

Adaptation stages. Table 2 isolates the contribution of each stage of proposer learning. In-context harness editing improves on the fixed initial harness on twelve of the thirteen tasks (all except PRISM), and training the proposer’s weights improves further over in-context adaptation on eleven, ties on AHC039, and is slightly lower only on EPLB (−0.47%-0.47\%). This highlights the importance of training the proposer’s weights rather than relying on in-context adaptation alone.

\para

Model scale. We scale up the proposer and the executor by replacing Qwen3.5-9B with Qwen3.8-27B. Because the 27B model is more expensive to run, we reduce the number of harnesses sampled per round from 32 to 8 and the evaluator calls per rollout from 20 to 5. Even with this smaller budget, the 27B model improves over the 9B baseline on ten of the thirteen tasks, ties on CP26 and PRISM, and is lower only on Hadamard (Table 2). Counting TriMul (1261.4 to 1096.4 μ\mus; Table 3), it improves on eleven of the fourteen tasks.

\para

Weak-to-strong transfer. Because the learned harness is explicit and separate from the executor’s weights, it can be moved to a stronger executor without retraining. In the spirit of weak-to-strong generalization [7], we take the harnesses learned with Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B, replace the executor with GPT-5.5, and continue search (HarnessTTT-Transfer). Table 3 compares both variants with the strongest reported result on each task, regardless of backbone or method. With transfer, HarnessTTT matches or exceeds this frontier on nine of fourteen tasks (seven excluding the quarantined LLM-SQL and Txn), is within 1%1\% on four more, and remains behind only on EPLB. It sets new best values on AC2 (0.9636 vs. 0.9629), AHC039 (571,450 vs. 567,503), AHC058, TriMul (1094.8 vs. 1183.0 μ\mus), and V2, and ties the frontier on Hadamard and PRISM. Transfer helps most where the small executor falls short: with GPT-5.5, the 9B harness raises AHC058 from 713.55 to 849.68 and Hadamard from 0.921 to 0.936. The transferred harnesses encode search strategies, such as layered construction and filling edge space first, that are not tied to the executor used during optimization, so discovery procedures can be reused across executors without transferring executor weights. Because executor choice and extra search are part of the transfer procedure, these gains do not isolate a pure transfer effect; §4.5 replays a fixed harness on a fixed executor set.

4.3 Ablation Study

\para

Comparison of reward-update locations. A rollout reward can update the executor’s weights, the proposer’s context, or the proposer’s weights. We compare the three routes on two tasks with the same base checkpoint, evaluator, initial harness, seed program, and 20 evaluator calls per executor trajectory. The executor arm is a budget-scaled TTT-Discover-style reference that keeps the initial harness and updates the executor with a three-epoch rank-64 LoRA on K=16K{=}16 final-edit trajectories per batch. The proposer arm trains a persistent rank-64 LoRA for three epochs on K=8K{=}8 proposals. The context arm makes no gradient update and adds two frozen-model analyst calls after the cold round. Because each harness candidate also costs a proposer rollout, Figure 5a plots every arm against total rollouts. A harness round spends 8 proposer and 8 executor rollouts; the executor arm has no proposer, so it runs 16 executor trajectories per round, and every arm reaches 320 rollouts after 20 rounds. The proposer arm reaches the highest endpoint on both tasks and gets there sooner. By 128 rollouts it has reached 1.00 on Erdős and 0.90 on autocorrelation II (normalized), while the context arm is at 0.34 and 0.41, and the executor arm is still below the plotted range on Erdős and at 0.26 on autocorrelation II. Updating the proposer thus turns rollout rewards into better search procedures early in the run.

\para

Test-time scaling. We study how discovery performance changes with search width and depth by varying the number of harness proposals per round, K∈{2,4,8,16,32}K\in\{2,4,8,16,32\}, and running each configuration for 15 outer rounds on CP26 and Hadamard (Figure 5b). The widest configuration, K=32K=32, achieves the highest final score on both tasks: 2.515 on CP26 and 0.812 on Hadamard, compared with 2.074 and 0.573 for the best narrower configurations, respectively. It also makes substantial late-stage improvements on both tasks, while the narrower configurations largely plateau.

\para

Reward design. Figure 5c varies only the proposer objective, with the same frozen executor, initial harness, seed program, budget, and K=32K{=}32 over 15 rounds; scores are normalized as in Figure 5a. Updating the proposer helps under either objective, and ours helps most: with the RLOO endpoint at 1.00, GRPO reaches 0.38 on CP26 and 0.26 on Hadamard, and the frozen proposer 0.14 and 0.21. GRPO’s curve is nearly flat after round 4 on both tasks, whereas RLOO keeps improving. This is consistent with §3.1: without division by the group standard deviation, near-tied groups no longer turn evaluator noise into large advantages, and max-sharpening concentrates credit on the candidate the round keeps. Each condition is a single campaign.

4.4 Effect of the Initial Program

\para

Different initial programs. The campaigns in §4.2 all start from the seed program of each task, so we first ask how the search depends on that starting point. Figure 6a runs HarnessTTT-9B on autocorrelation II from two programs: the default seed and the stronger initial program released with ThetaEvolve (StrongInit)22 2 https://github.com/ypwang61/ThetaEvolve/blob/main/Results/SecondAutoCorrIneq/programs/StrongInit.py. Both runs improve over 15 rounds, from 0.896 to 0.922 and from 0.909 to 0.930. The default-seed run passes StrongInit’s starting score by round 3, and the gap between the two runs narrows from 0.013 to 0.007. It does not close, however, so the final score still depends on the initial program.

\para

Continuing from strong programs. Figure 6b asks whether the search still helps when the starting program is already strong. On autocorrelation II, starting from a ThetaEvolve RL@65 program at 0.941, HarnessTTT reaches 0.948, whereas the frozen initial harness reaches only 0.942 from the same program. Almost all of this gain arrives in the first round. On Erdős, starting from the best program of the HarnessTTT-27B campaign (0.380902), the search lowers c5c_{5} to 0.380868 and improves in most rounds. The remaining headroom is small in both cases, and the Erdős result is still above the reported frontier of 0.380859 (Table 3).

4.5 Cross-Executor Replay of Learned Harnesses

Because the learned harness is explicit, it can be replayed on executors it was never optimized with. We fix the harnesses learned with Qwen3.5-9B (the evolved harness) and swap the executor for GLM-5.2, GLM-5.1 [15], GPT-5.3 [44], Qwen-235B [69], or GPT-OSS-120B [43], without using any of their outcomes to train the proposer. For each executor, OpenEvolve [58] runs 48 iterations from the initial or the evolved harness under identical settings, and NexAU [41] records tool use over three decode seeds. The evolved harness raises the eleven-task mean normalized score on all five executors by +1.2+1.2 to +13.4+13.4 points (+5.4+5.4 on average; Figure 7). The gains track custom-tool use: Qwen-235B calls the generated tools most often (19.9 attempts per 100 turns) and gains the most (+13.4+13.4), followed by GPT-5.3 (9.9; +5.7+5.7). The harness thus carries a reusable search procedure that other executors can execute, without proposer retraining or executor-weight updates; with one search seed per executor, these gains are descriptive point estimates.

5 Conclusion

We introduced HarnessTTT, which casts test-time discovery as learning the harness rather than the model: a proposer is trained online to write executable harnesses for a frozen executor. With a frozen 9B executor, HarnessTTT improves on OpenEvolve and Finch-9B on all eleven benchmark tasks and holds the best open-weight (≤\leq10B) value on nine; a 27B model improves further on eleven of fourteen tasks; and with transfer to GPT-5.5 it matches or exceeds the reported frontier on nine of fourteen tasks and comes within 1%1\% on four more. Ablations show that, at matched rollouts, updating the proposer’s weights reaches better results earlier than updating the executor or the context, and that RLOO with max-sharpening outperforms GRPO and a frozen proposer. Together, these results show that harness search can itself be learned at test time, complementary to scaling the model that executes it.

  2. 2.

  5. 5.

Appendix B HarnessTTT on one page

Figure 2 summarizes HarnessTTT on a single page. Panel (a) contrasts two test-time evolution loops that differ only in what the reward updates. In executor RL, as in TTT-Discover [77], the executor θ\theta samples NN rollouts, each covering one strategy; the reward updates θ\theta, and the final weights θ⋆\theta^{\star} cannot be transferred. In HarnessTTT, the proposer ϕ\phi writes KK harnesses—named, readable files for the prompt, skills, tools, and middleware—that the frozen executor M0M_{0} rolls out. A single harness-guided rollout can move through several strategies (A→\toB→\toC). Candidates are scored and gated, the reward updates only ϕ\phi, and the best harness H⋆H^{\star} is a transferable package. Panel (b) lists the four properties that follow. Exploration happens within a rollout. Every edit is traceable as a named file. Generated code is kept safe by schema, scope, and sandbox checks. The harness transfers to other frozen executors.

Panel (c) marks the tasks on which the learned harness, with or without transfer, matches or exceeds the strongest reported system of any backbone (Table 3). It exceeds the frontier on seven tasks: AC2 against Hyra [21]; AHC039, AHC058, TriMul, and V2 against SimpleTES [72]; LLM-SQL against LEVI [63]; and Txn against CORAL [48]. It ties the frontier on Hadamard (SimpleTES) and on PRISM (OpenEvolve [58], ShinkaEvolve [28], CORAL, and LEVI). LLM-SQL and Txn are quarantined. On four more tasks, it is within 1%1\% of the frontier: Erdős and AC1 (Hyra), circle packing (CORAL; EurekAgent [68]), and scRNA (SimpleTES). It remains behind only on EPLB (LEVI).

Panel (d) shows the task-specific harnesses the proposer writes on four tasks, with the executor frozen. Each card gives the goal, the visible effect on the solution, and the generated tool and skill or middleware: a staggered-packing constructor and packing guide for circle packing, a basin-and-bottleneck analyzer with a multi-start strategy for Hadamard, a column-ranking tool and row-sorting playbook for LLM-SQL, and a conflict-graph builder with graph-first middleware for transaction scheduling. Panel (e) follows one circle-packing (n=26n{=}26) campaign with a 9B proposer and executor. Named harness edits raise the sum of radii from 0.960 at the seed to 1.467 in round 1 (broaden the search), 2.235 in round 5 (test four layouts), 2.278 in round 7 (escape a plateau), and 2.541 in round 10 (import a warm start). Replayed unchanged on a frozen GLM-5.2 executor, the same harness reaches 2.635984 in all nine runs, within 0.001%0.001\% of the reported frontier (2.6360 by CORAL [48]; 2.635999 by EurekAgent [68]).

Appendix C The harness spec language

The proposer’s output is a harness spec: a declarative document that fixes every component the frozen executor sees (Figure 8). A candidate spec is a partial YAML document merged over its parent spec. Fields the candidate sets override the parent’s, and fields it omits are inherited. A proposal that rewrites only the skill playbook therefore still defines a complete harness, and what a candidate changes can be read directly from the fields it sets. Table 4 lists the fields.

\para

Overriding existing components. The upper block rewrites what the executor reads and how it is run. Three text fields carry the natural-language part of the harness. The system prompt sets the executor’s workflow. The skill package is split into a short card that advertises the skill in the executor’s tool list and a playbook body that holds the procedure itself. tool_descriptions rewrites how the fixed tools are described without touching their code, so the proposer can steer when and how the executor calls them. sampling and agent set the decoding parameters and the iteration cap. middleware tunes the built-in controls: when the budget reminder starts, when a stalled run is restarted and how many restarts are allowed, and the output-truncation limit.

\para

Changing the component set. The lower block adds or removes components. A candidate may add up to three tools, each with a name, a description, a JSON schema for its arguments, and a Python implementation. It may also add up to two skill packages, and up to two middlewares, each attached to a named hook with its own Python implementation. Tools can be removed only if they are marked optional. These caps bound how much new code a single candidate can introduce.

\para

Constraints on generated code. Generated tool names must match ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{2,31}$: they start with a lowercase letter, contain 3–32 lowercase letters, digits, or underscores, and may not shadow a reserved name. Each generated implementation is limited to 6,000 characters. A generated tool exposes the single run(ctx, args) entry point and reaches the task only through ctx (Appendix D). Before it is mounted, it must pass the static gates and sandboxed self-test of §3.2. A tool that still fails after repair is dropped rather than shipped.

\para

Validation, compilation, and hashing. Validation is fail-closed: anything that does not pass is excluded rather than let through. The proposer calls validate_harness, which checks component mounts, field schemas, and generated code, and finishes with submit_harness (§3). A deterministic materializer then merges the candidate over its parent, compiles the result into a runnable package bound by agent.yaml, and writes a canonical spec of the effective harness. Within one materializer revision, identical effective specs yield identical canonical-spec bytes and therefore the same hash. Provenance metadata stored with the package may still differ, so the hash identifies the effective harness rather than any particular package. Because the hash is taken after merging, two candidates in a group that reach the same effective harness through different partial documents share a hash. The hash is used to de-duplicate them.

Appendix D Capability surface of generated tools

A generated tool touches the task only through the ctx object passed to its run(ctx, args) entry point (Table 5). Through this interface a tool can read the current and best programs, stage edits, score them, and read the task’s inputs. It cannot see how the scores are computed.

\para

Scoring and budget. The two scoring calls differ in cost and accounting. evaluate() runs the full evaluation and uses one of the BB evaluator calls. probe() scores the program on a subsample at roughly one-eighth the cost. It does not count toward BB, but it has its own cap. A tool can therefore screen edits cheaply and save budgeted calls for promising ones, but the cap stops it from using probes as unlimited free evaluations.

\para

Isolation. Path resolution refuses evaluator and ground-truth locations. The configured sandbox gives generated tools no network, general-filesystem, or subprocess access.

\para

Static gate and self-test. The static gate admits imports only from math, re, json, itertools, functools, collections, heapq, bisect, random, statistics, string, typing, dataclasses, numpy, and pandas. It also applies the forbidden-access checks of §3.2. A tool that passes the gate then runs a self-test against a mock context under RLIMIT_CPU 20 s and RLIMIT_AS 6 GB.

\para

Verifiability. The public artifact does not currently include the trusted runtime, sandbox, gate, scrubber, localization guard, or served-model request logs. These settings therefore describe the evaluated protocol and cannot yet be verified independently.

Appendix E Proposer training details

Table 6 gives the configuration of both proposer-training campaigns: the Qwen3.5-9B campaigns of §4.2, and the Qwen3.8-27B campaign whose harnesses Appendix G lists. The two campaigns share the search, reward, and update recipe. They differ only in model scale, proposals per round, the evaluator budget per rollout, and the reference score uτu_{\tau} (Appendix F). The paragraphs below explain how the pieces fit together.

Round structure.

Each task runs for 20 outer rounds. In each round the proposer samples KK harnesses, and each candidate harness is rolled out once by the frozen executor and compared against the shared incumbent score. A round therefore launches 2​K2K agent trajectories (one proposer episode and one candidate rollout per candidate): 16 in the 27B campaign and 64 in the 9B campaigns. To limit the cost of the larger executor, the 27B campaign samples K=8K=8 proposals rather than 32. It also gives each rollout B=5B=5 evaluator calls of up to 420 s, where the 9B campaigns give B=20B=20 calls of up to 600 s. Every rollout is capped at 3 h of wall-clock time. A round is accepted only if at least six of its proposals validate (the min6 gate). The same frozen model may repair a generated tool that fails validation at most twice.

Parent selection and grouping.

Programs and harnesses are promoted separately. The program registry is a strict single-program ratchet: a rollout’s program replaces the incumbent only if it strictly improves the score. The incumbent harness is promoted only when the round’s best candidate exceeds the historical best; displaced parents are archived. From the second round on, the KK proposal slots are dealt round-robin to a beam of two parents: the promoted or retained incumbent, and the best candidate within 2% of the top score that adds a new component (or else the second-highest scorer). An advantage group contains the proposals that share one sampling condition (parent spec, prompt, and budget hash). Hence Kg=KK_{g}=K in the first round and K/2K/2 afterwards, which is 8 and then 4 for the 27B campaign, and 32 and then 16 for the 9B campaigns.

Rewards and advantages.

Both campaigns compare each candidate with the shared incumbent score bτb_{\tau}. Below the reference,

gk=sk−bτuτ−bτ,rk={3​tanh⁡(gk/3)gk>0,max⁡(−1,gk)gk≤0,g_{k}=\frac{s_{k}-b_{\tau}}{u_{\tau}-b_{\tau}},\qquad r_{k}=\begin{cases}3\tanh(g_{k}/3)&g_{k}>0,\\ \max(-1,\,g_{k})&g_{k}\leq 0,\end{cases}

as in Eqs. 1 and 2. Here uτu_{\tau} is the reference score of Appendix F. The positive branch compresses large gains smoothly, and the negative branch keeps regressions linear down to −1-1. Invalid, failed, or repaired candidates receive rk=−1r_{k}=-1, so they cannot earn credit for a gain. Among the creditable candidates, rewards within δ=10−3\delta=10^{-3} of each other are collapsed to their mean. The advantage then follows Eq. 3 with group size KgK_{g}: Ak=0.7​AkLOO+0.3​(softmax⁡(r/T)k−1/Kg)A_{k}=0.7\,A^{\mathrm{LOO}}_{k}+0.3\,\big(\operatorname{softmax}(r/T)_{k}-1/K_{g}\big) with T=max⁡(range⁡(r)/4, 10−9)T=\max(\mathrm{range}(r)/4,\,10^{-9}). A group whose candidates are all valid and tied carries no signal and is excluded (Ak=0A_{k}=0), as is a group in which every candidate receives the same status penalty; mixed groups keep the contrast between tied valid rewards and status penalties.

Proposer update.

Training runs on slime with the FSDP backend on 8 GPUs, for three epochs per round over all trainable episodes of the round. Each episode is converted into a replay of its full multi-turn trajectory, and the loss mask covers assistant turns that are closed by a later user or tool message. Episodes are truncated to 18,000 tokens in a terminal-preserving way: tool observations are clipped first, and then the longest fitting suffix that starts at an assistant action is kept. The rewarded submit_harness action therefore always survives truncation. The loss is a clipped policy-gradient objective with the precomputed advantage AkA_{k} broadcast over the masked tokens. slime’s own reward normalization is disabled, consistent with the absence of variance scaling in Eq. 3. A KL penalty of 0.1 (low_var_kl) anchors the policy to the frozen base. The adapter is cumulative: each round loads only the weights of the previous round’s adapter (--load-weights-only). Every round’s checkpoint is retained. The merged checkpoint is served as the next round’s proposer, while the executor stays at the base checkpoint.

Appendix F Published reference scores

The reward of §3.1 divides a candidate’s gain over its baseline (the incumbent score bτb_{\tau}; Appendix E) by the baseline’s remaining gap to a task reference uτu_{\tau}. The reference therefore sets the scale of credit on each task; it is not a target that the proposer or the executor ever sees.

In the 27B campaign, uτu_{\tau} is the largest of four fixed values: the seed score, the best human value, the published ≤\leq10B SOTA, and the Finch-9B score. All four are expressed in the evaluator’s combined score. Table 7 lists the resulting references. The 9B campaigns use the published ≤\leq10B SOTA alone (Table 1), which changes the reference on the four tasks where the best human value is largest: Erdős, Hadamard, AHC039, and AHC058. When uτu_{\tau} does not exceed the baseline, the remaining gap is not positive. The reward then falls back to the relative gain over |bτ||b_{\tau}|, clipped to [−1,5][-1,5]. The reference enters the reward only. It is never written into a harness, a prompt, or a tool, and a leak guard rejects any proposal or repair whose text contains it.

Appendix G Discovered harnesses

This section lists the final incumbent harness that the trained Qwen3.8-27B proposer produced on two of its evolution tasks, circle packing and Erdős minimum overlap (20 rounds each). The final harness is the package that the last round’s collector retained as the parent. Table 8 summarizes the two harnesses. For each task we then give the lineage of the final harness and excerpts of the compiled artifacts on disk: the effective spec with long bodies replaced by pointers, the generated tool code, the generated skill playbooks, and, for circle packing, the policy sections the proposer wrote into the executor’s system prompt.

Both harnesses keep the base configuration: sampling at T=0.7T{=}0.7, top-pp 0.95, top-kk 20, and at most 8,192 tokens; 36 executor iterations; and the base middleware thresholds (budget reminder from 3 evaluations left, stall restart after 8 stalls, at most 2 restarts, tool output clipped at 8,000 characters). The proposer’s edits went into the prompt, the skills, and the tools.

G.1 Circle packing (n=26n{=}26): a verifier and a transform in front of every evaluation

The lineage (Table G.1) shows the harness being assembled in the order a human engineer might choose. A feasibility checker comes first (round 0), then a construction playbook that tells the executor how to use it (round 5), then a transform that proposes repaired geometry (round 6), and finally a first-moves policy that stops the executor from discarding the incumbent’s optimizer (rounds 8 and 13). The checker, packing_feasibility (Listing ), uses a water-filling relaxation to return the largest radii consistent with the walls and every pair, so the executor can rank layouts and repair the listed breaches without spending an evaluation. Seven further generated tools proposed in rounds 1–19 (packing_repair, packing_variant_generator, local_packing_optimizer, packing_family_scan, …) were rolled out but are not part of the final harness.
